lede: A basket holds several products, a post several tags, an API response several line items. Arrays keep those lists in one row; `explode` turns each element into a row of its own so you can work with them one by one.
objectives: Turn each array element into its own row with `F.explode`, and keep empty arrays with `F.explode_outer`
Build arrays from columns with `F.array` and `F.array_repeat`, and explode an array of structs into columns
Check and tidy arrays with `F.array_contains`, `F.array_distinct` and `F.sort_array`

blocks.md:
The shop's tables keep one value per cell, but data often arrives with lists inside. Suppose the mobile app sends each basket as an order id with a list of product ids. The examples build small DataFrames like that with `spark.createDataFrame`; `products` and `order_items` are loaded as usual, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

`F.explode(col)` makes **one row per element** of the array. The other selected columns are repeated on each of those rows.

blocks.title: One row per product in a basket
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

baskets = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("O00001", ["P005", "P005", "P004"]), ("O00002", ["P001"]), ("O00003", ["P001", "P007", "P003"])],
    "order_id STRING, product_ids ARRAY<STRING>",
)
baskets.show(truncate=False)

baskets.select("order_id", F.explode("product_ids").alias("product_id")).show()
blocks.note: Three baskets become seven rows, one per element, and `order_id` repeats on each. Repeated elements, like O00001's two P005s, give two rows.

blocks.md: A row whose array is empty or missing has no elements, so `explode` gives it **no rows**: it disappears. When every row must survive, use `F.explode_outer`, which gives such a row once, with NULL for the element.

blocks.title: Empty and missing arrays
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

baskets = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("O00001", ["P005", "P004"]), ("O00013", []), ("O00014", None)],
    "order_id STRING, product_ids ARRAY<STRING>",
)

baskets.select("order_id", F.explode("product_ids").alias("product_id")).show()
baskets.select("order_id", F.explode_outer("product_ids").alias("product_id")).show()
blocks.note: With `explode`, O00013 and O00014 vanish. With `explode_outer` each stays as one row with a NULL `product_id`.

blocks.md:
`F.posexplode(col)` also gives each element's position, starting at 0. It makes two columns, so name both at once: `.alias("pos", "product_id")`.

You can build arrays from columns too. `F.array("a", "b")` puts several columns of the same type into one array. `F.array_repeat(value, n)` repeats a value `n` times, and `n` can be a column, so `F.array_repeat("product_id", "quantity")` lists a product once per unit ordered.

blocks.title: Positions, and one row per unit
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

units = order_items.select("order_id", "line_no", F.array_repeat("product_id", "quantity").alias("units"))
units.show(3, truncate=False)

units.select("order_id", "line_no", F.posexplode("units").alias("pos", "product_id")).show(7)
blocks.note: O00001's first line ordered 3 units of P005, so its array repeats P005 three times and explodes into positions 0, 1 and 2. A quantity of 0 would give an empty array, and no rows.

blocks.md:
Arrays can hold structs, as JSON line items often do. Exploding gives one struct per row, and `"col.*"` from the structs lesson spreads its fields into columns.

To put a fixed value into a struct, `F.lit(value)` makes a column holding that same value on every row. Building an array of labelled structs and exploding it turns several columns into rows, a common way to reshape a wide table into a long one.

blocks.title: Explode an array of structs
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

long = products.select(
    "product_id",
    F.explode(F.array(
        F.struct(F.lit("name").alias("field"), F.col("name").alias("value")),
        F.struct(F.lit("category").alias("field"), F.col("category").alias("value")),
    )).alias("entry"),
)
long.printSchema()
long.select("product_id", "entry.*").show()
blocks.note: Eight products become sixteen rows: each product's name and category, labelled by `field`. Every struct in an array must have the same fields and types.

blocks.md:
Some questions don't need exploding at all; functions work on the whole array:

- `F.array_contains(col, value)`: true if the value is in the array.
- `F.array_distinct(col)`: the array without repeats, in first-seen order.
- `F.sort_array(col)`: sorted ascending (`asc=False` for descending).
- `F.size(col)`: how many elements, as before.

blocks.title: Work on the whole array
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

baskets = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("O00001", ["P005", "P005", "P004"]), ("O00003", ["P001", "P007", "P003"]), ("O00008", ["P004", "P002", "P004"])],
    "order_id STRING, product_ids ARRAY<STRING>",
)

baskets.select(
    "order_id",
    F.array_contains("product_ids", "P004").alias("has_p004"),
    F.array_distinct("product_ids").alias("distinct_ids"),
    F.sort_array("product_ids").alias("sorted_ids"),
    F.size(F.array_distinct("product_ids")).alias("different"),
).show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: Every row stays a single row. O00008 has P004 twice, so it has two different products, not three.

concept.prompt: A DataFrame has three rows with arrays of 2, 0 and 3 elements. How many rows does `select("id", F.explode("items"))` return?
choices: An error, because one array is empty
concept.why: One row per element: 2 + 0 + 3 = 5. The row with an empty array disappears; `explode_outer` would keep it as one row with NULL, giving 6.

concept.prompt: What positions does `F.posexplode` give for an array of three elements?
concept.why: Positions start at 0, like array indexes.

concept.prompt: What does `F.array_repeat("product_id", "quantity")` give on a line with quantity 0?
choices: An empty array, so exploding it gives no rows
concept.why: Repeating a value zero times gives an empty array, which `explode` turns into no rows.

review: `F.explode(col)` gives one row per array element; the other selected columns repeat.
`explode` drops rows whose array is empty or missing; `explode_outer` keeps them with NULL.
`F.array(...)` builds an array from columns; `F.array_repeat(value, n)` repeats a value `n` times.
Explode an array of structs, then use `"col.*"` to spread the fields; `F.lit` puts a fixed value in a column.
`array_contains`, `array_distinct`, `sort_array` and `size` work on the whole array without exploding.
